entities.name: Justice and Development Party
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Justice and Development Party (Adalet ve Kalkınma Partisi, AKP) of Turkey, founded in 2001 by Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and Abdullah Gül, has governed Turkey continuously since its 2002 electoral landslide — the longest continuous single-party government in Turkish democratic history. The AKP's first decade (2002-2013) was praised for economic growth (GDP tripled), EU accession negotiations, and reduced military influence over politics; the second decade became increasingly authoritarian following the 2013 Gezi Park protests and the 2016 coup attempt.

Erdoğan founded the AKP after being released from prison (where he had served 4 months for reciting a religious poem deemed to incite hatred) from the ashes of the banned Islamist Welfare Party. The AKP positioned itself as 'Muslim democrats' analogous to European Christian Democrats — combining Islamic conservatism with liberal economics and pro-EU orientation. The 2002 election gave the AKP 34% of votes but 66% of seats due to Turkey's 10% electoral threshold.

Turkey's GDP tripled during AKP's first decade, inflation fell, and Turkey became a G20 economy. The 2013 Gezi Park protests marked the turning point: Erdoğan's response was increasingly authoritarian, culminating in the 2016 failed coup attempt (15,000 killed, 50,000 arrested in its aftermath), constitutional referendum centralizing power in Erdoğan's hands (2017), and Turkey's downgrade to 'Not Free' by Freedom House. The AKP represents the global pattern of democratically elected parties gradually dismantling democratic norms.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The AKP represents the defining case study of how a democratically elected moderate Islamist party can gradually dismantle democratic institutions through legitimate-seeming constitutional changes — Turkey's democratic regression under Erdoğan became the template for understanding 21st-century autocratic backsliding.
